Please read this carefully:

<document>
# Hours, Output and the Pilot Problem: A Re-examination of the Halden Reduced-Hours Pilot

*Comment, Journal of Labour and Organisation Studies. K. Varga and T. Holm, Centre for Applied Labour Statistics.*

## Abstract

The Halden pilot reported that 61 organisations maintained output while cutting scheduled hours by 20%, implying a 23.4% gain in output per hour. Using the pilot's microdata, released under the Institute's data-sharing policy, we re-examine the result. Four problems, each documented below, account for most of the reported gain: attrition that was not random, a manager-reported output measure that overstates output relative to organisations' own records, an hours denominator that counts scheduled rather than actual time, and an unadjusted revenue comparison. Correcting the first three, the gain in output per hour falls from 23.4% to 10.8% in the subset of organisations where correction is possible. We then argue that the remaining gain is plausibly a novelty effect, and that the per-hour productivity gains reported for reduced-hours schemes are, in our assessment, entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty.

## 1. Attrition

The working paper states that nine of the 70 enrolled organisations "withdrew during the preparation phase, chiefly for scheduling reasons". The microdata tell a different story. Seven of the nine withdrew after the reduced schedule had begun: four in the first month and three in the second. In exit forms, six of the nine gave workload or inability to maintain output as the main reason, and two gave scheduling. The organisations that found the change hardest were therefore removed from the sample before the outcome was measured. With nine of 70 organisations missing, and those nine plausibly the least successful, the reported sample of 61 is a sample of survivors.

## 2. The output measure

The primary outcome was an index completed by a manager who was also the pilot's internal sponsor. Managers were asked to base the index on organisational records, but were not required to submit them. Twenty-three organisations did submit underlying records (billable hours delivered, tickets closed, units produced, or cases completed). For these 23 we can compare the manager's index with the index implied by the records.

**Table 1. Manager-reported and record-based output, 23 organisations with records**

| Measure | Mean output index (baseline = 100) |
|---|---|
| Manager-reported index | 98.9 |
| Index computed from submitted records | 95.1 |
| Difference | −3.8 points |

In 19 of the 23 organisations the manager-reported index exceeded the record-based index. We do not suggest bad faith. A manager responsible for a change he or she advocated, asked to rate its effect on a scale where 100 means "unchanged", will tend to round toward success. But the difference is systematic, and the headline output figure of 98.7 should not be taken at face value.

## 3. The hours denominator

The pilot computed output per hour by dividing output by the ratio of scheduled hours, 0.8. Twenty-seven organisations used time-tracking software throughout. Their data show average actual weekly hours of 40.3 at baseline and 34.6 during the pilot, a fall of 14.1% rather than 20%. The difference comes from two sources visible in the logs: longer working days on the remaining four days (average +0.7 hours per day), and work logged on the scheduled day off (on average 1.6 hours per week). Some further work on the day off is probably not logged.

Seventeen organisations have both submitted output records and time tracking. In this subset, record-based output was 95.4 and actual hours fell from 40.4 to 34.8 (−13.9%). The implied gain in output per actual hour is 10.8% (95.4 / 86.1), less than half the reported 23.4%.

**Table 2. Implied gain in output per hour under successive corrections**

| Specification | Output | Hours ratio | Gain per hour |
|---|---|---|---|
| As reported (all 61) | 98.7 | 0.800 | +23.4% |
| Record-based output, scheduled hours (23) | 95.1 | 0.800 | +18.9% |
| Manager-reported output, actual hours (27) | 98.4 | 0.859 | +14.6% |
| Record-based output, actual hours (17) | 95.4 | 0.861 | +10.8% |

## 4. Revenue

The working paper reports revenue 1.4% higher than in the previous year. This is a nominal comparison. Consumer prices rose by 4.1% over the same twelve months; in real terms, revenue in participating organisations fell by approximately 2.6%. Revenue is in any case a poor proxy for productivity, but the figure as presented gives a misleading impression of growth.

## 5. Sectoral claims

The pilot concluded that gains in output per hour were "found in every sector" and that the model is "sector-general". This conclusion is an artifact of the per-hour metric. When hours are cut by 20%, any output index above 80 will register as a per-hour gain. Retail and hospitality output fell by 6.9% on the manager-reported measure; the three retail and hospitality organisations among the 23 with records show a fall of 11.2%. A fall in output of this size in a customer-facing business is not evidence that reduced hours work there. The Varden County trial's counter and contact-centre stratum, the only randomised evidence on coverage-bound work, found a fall in output per employee of 11.4% and longer waits for the public. That is, in our view, the most reliable finding in the literature to date.

## 6. Novelty

After the corrections above, a gain in output per actual hour of about 11% remains in the subset of survivors with usable data. We think this residual should not be read as a durable effect. The pilot's own survey shows self-reported energy at work rising by 0.61 standard deviations at month three and falling to 0.29 at month six. Extrapolating this decline, energy would return to baseline at around month ten. A change that staff chose, welcomed and knew to be under evaluation is the classic setting for a novelty effect: effort rises while the change is new and observed, and falls back once it is routine. Six months is not long enough to distinguish a novelty effect from a durable one, and the burden of proof lies with those claiming the latter.

## 7. The meetings hypothesis

The Varden trial's authors report, in an unregistered exploratory analysis, that cuts in recurring meetings correlated with per-hour gains across seven treated offices, and suggest this as a mechanism. We regard this as a post hoc account fitted to a subgroup. A correlation across seven offices, selected for analysis after the results were known, is precisely the kind of finding that does not replicate. The meetings explanation has an intuitive appeal that has outrun its evidence, and it should not be cited as a mechanism.

## 8. Conclusion

Taking the problems together: attrition removed the organisations least able to cope; the output measure overstated output by roughly four points; the hours measure overstated the reduction in time by roughly six points; and the remaining gain coincides with a decaying measure of enthusiasm. We conclude that the per-hour productivity gains reported for reduced-hours schemes are, in our assessment, entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty, and that the best-supported finding is the negative one: where output depends on presence, reduced hours reduce output.

We recommend that future evaluations use record-based output, actual hours, a randomised or at least matched comparison group, follow-up of at least eighteen months, and analysis of all enrolled organisations including those that withdraw.

## Data note

All re-analyses use the Halden pilot microdata (release 1.2). The corrections in Table 2 can only be computed for subsets of organisations, and those subsets were not chosen at random; organisations with time tracking and records may differ from the others. Our corrected estimates therefore describe those subsets, not the pilot as a whole.

</document>
response:
I read the whole comment. Its first half is strong: it checks the pilot's claims against the pilot's own microdata and finds real problems. Its conclusion does not follow from that work. The authors find a corrected gain of about 11%, then declare all per-hour gains to be "entirely an artifact." To do that they rely on a two-point extrapolation and leave out the one randomised result that measured exactly what they recommend measuring.

## Arithmetic check

**These reproduce:**
- Table 2: 95.1 / 0.8 = +18.9%; 98.4 / 0.859 = +14.6%; 95.4 / 0.861 = +10.8%.
- Hours: 34.6 / 40.3 = 0.859 (−14.1%); 34.8 / 40.4 = 0.861 (−13.9%).
- Real revenue: 1.014 / 1.041 = 0.974, i.e. −2.6%.

**These don't:**
- **The hours breakdown doesn't add up.** Four scheduled days of 8 hours plus 0.7 extra hours a day gives 34.8 hours. Adding 1.6 hours of day-off work gives 36.4, not 34.6. Starting from the baseline day of 8.06 hours gives 36.6. Either the components or the total is wrong, and that matters because the total drives every per-hour correction.
- **The energy extrapolation is off.** A straight line from 0.61 at month three to 0.29 at month six reaches zero at about month 8.7, not "around month ten." The bigger problem is that a line through two points tells you very little, as discussed under point 4.

## What's valuable

- **The attrition finding is the most serious result.** The working paper said nine organisations withdrew "during the preparation phase, chiefly for scheduling reasons." If the microdata show that seven withdrew after the schedule began, mostly over workload, the original paper misdescribed its sample. The Halden authors should be asked to respond.
- **The manager-versus-records comparison is well designed.** The manager's figure was higher in 19 of 23 cases. A sign test gives p ≈ 0.001, so the gap is systematic and not chance.
- **The scheduled-versus-actual hours correction is right.** It matches the Varden trial's own warning about scheduled hours.
- **The real-terms revenue correction and the point about the per-hour metric are both correct.**
- **The recommendations are sound:** record-based output, actual hours, a comparison group, longer follow-up, and inclusion of withdrawals.

## Main issues

**1. The conclusion ignores the Varden case-processing result.**
The comment treats Varden's counter stratum as "the most reliable finding in the literature." The same trial's case-processing stratum found output per *actual* hour up 12.5% (95% CI +6.9 to +18.4). That estimate already meets every standard the comment sets:
- It was randomised, so self-selection and survivorship don't apply.
- Output came from administrative records, not manager ratings.
- Hours came from timesheets, not schedules.
- It ran for nine months, longer than the six months the comment calls too short.

Even Varden's counter stratum shows +6.7% per actual hour. You can't cite one stratum of a trial as the most reliable evidence and ignore the other stratum when it contradicts your conclusion. Varden's real weaknesses (few clusters, staff knowing their assignment) are reasons for caution. They are not grounds for "entirely an artifact."

**2. The abstract says the attrition was corrected, but it wasn't.**
The abstract says "correcting the first three" problems gives 10.8%. Table 2 corrects only the output measure and the hours denominator. Attrition isn't adjusted anywhere, and probably can't be without outcome data for the nine organisations that withdrew.

The direction of the bias is plausible: including withdrawals would likely lower the estimate further. But its size is unknown. Bounding methods would show how much attrition *could* matter, such as worst-case or Lee bounds, or an intention-to-treat analysis that assigns withdrawals plausible output values. The same applies to the abstract's "four problems … account for most of the reported gain": revenue never enters the per-hour calculation, so it can't account for any of the gain.

**3. Table 2 changes the sample at every step.**
The rows use 61, 23, 27 and 17 organisations. Each step mixes the effect of the correction with the effect of changing which organisations are included. The table should be run on the 17 organisations that have both records and time-tracking:
- manager index with scheduled hours;
- record index with scheduled hours;
- manager index with actual hours;
- record index with actual hours.

That would show how much each correction contributes on its own. The table also needs confidence intervals. Every estimate here comes from 17 to 27 organisations, and none has an uncertainty range.

**4. Novelty is asserted, not shown.**
- **The energy evidence is thin.** It is two survey points on self-reported energy, which is not output. Extrapolating a straight line assumes a steady decline. A drop that levels off fits the same two points equally well.
- **The Halden data could test it directly.** The output index was collected monthly. If novelty drives the per-hour gain, output should fall over months one to six, at least in the 17 organisations with record-based data. The comment doesn't look.
- **Novelty isn't an artifact.** A real but temporary improvement is different from a measurement or selection error. Calling everything "artifact" blurs that distinction.
- **The burden-of-proof argument cuts both ways.** "Six months can't distinguish novelty from a durable effect" is correct. It justifies agnosticism about the residual gain. It doesn't justify concluding there is none.

**5. The meetings critique misdescribes the Varden analysis.**
- The seven offices weren't "a subgroup selected for analysis after the results were known." They were the entire treated case-processing stratum, which was defined before randomisation. The legitimate criticisms are that the analysis wasn't registered, it has only seven offices, and there was no baseline measure of meetings.
- The Varden authors already said it "cannot establish a mechanism" and registered a confirmatory test. The comment's recommendation is something they had already adopted.
- If confirmed, the meetings mechanism would be a durable, non-novelty source of gains. It would directly contradict the "entirely an artifact" conclusion. That may be why it matters more than the comment allows. Halden's own interviews also reported meeting cuts at 47 of 58 organisations, so this is a reason to test the idea, not to discard it.

**6. "Record-based" output isn't automatically more accurate.**
One of the record types listed is "billable hours delivered," and that is an input, not an output. If staff work fewer hours, billable hours fall almost automatically. Including it would push the record-based index down for reasons unrelated to productivity. The comment should:
- break down the record types across the 23 organisations;
- show the manager-versus-records gap with billable-hours organisations excluded.

Records may also leave out quality improvements that a manager would reasonably count.

**7. The retail comparison is very small.**
The −11.2% figure comes from three organisations, which can't support a claim about a sector. The comparison with Varden is reasonable in direction. But Varden's counters were public-sector offices with fixed opening hours and no change in staffing, which is a specific setting.

## Smaller points

- **The claims escalate.** The abstract says "most" of the gain, then "plausibly novelty," then "entirely an artifact." The conclusion should match the strongest claim the evidence supports.
- **The conclusion mixes up two measures.** "Reduced hours reduce output" refers to output per employee. It doesn't contradict per-hour gains, and Varden shows both at once. The comment should say which measure each claim is about.
- **CPI may not be the right price index.** It measures consumer prices, not the prices these organisations charge. Producer or sector price indices would fit better, though the correction would probably still point the same way. Also, revenue came from only 52 organisations, and the comment doesn't state which subset it uses.
- **The data note contradicts the conclusion.** It correctly says the corrected figures "describe those subsets, not the pilot as a whole." The conclusion then generalises to all reduced-hours schemes.

## Bottom line

The defensible version of this comment would say the following. The Halden headline overstates the per-hour gain by more than half, its sample was distorted by attrition the paper misreported, and its sector-general claim is unsupported. A residual gain of about 11% remains in a non-random subset, and its durability is unknown.

That fits the Varden trial: real per-hour gains, smaller than the pilots claim, with output losses in coverage-bound work. "Entirely an artifact" fits neither the comment's own numbers nor the best available evidence.

I can draft a referee report on the comment, or a short reconciliation of all three papers showing what the combined evidence does and doesn't support.
